newsitem.title: GREECE: Past Greek budgets show target, outcomes diverging.
newsitem.headline: Past Greek budgets show target, outcomes diverging.

text.p: Greece announced plans on Friday to almost halve its budget deficit in a bid to qualify for EMU, but past experience shows that the country has found hitting its deficit targets is not easy.

A closer look at Greece's 1994-1996 budget performance shows that the central government budget deficit target has constantly diverged from the actual deficit by a large margin. The actual deficit has turned out to be higher than the initial target.
On the other hand, the central government primary surplus to GDP ratios have displayed a much more stable behaviour over the same period.

The contrasting behaviour of the overall central budget deficit and the primary surplus points to the accounting treatment of interest payments on public debt as a likely explanatory variable in the budget equation.
The general government budget deficit targets also diverged but the actual figures turned out to be lower than initial targets.
This can be largely explained by unrecorded operating surpluses of state entities mainly due to the 1992 social insurance reform that came to light in 1995.

But the central government budget and primary surplus figures are calculated on an administrative basis and the general government budget figures on a national accounts basis which means that a comparison of the two is not valid.
The central government budget figures do not include accrued and capitalised interest as well as the non-cash coverage of state guarantees to public sector utilities.

Another interesting development that has worked towards reducing budget deficits as a percent of GDP is the better-than- expected performance of the GDP which reflects upward revisions as well as a higher volume of goods and services in the economy.

National Economy Minister Yannos Papandoniou, describing his 1997 budget as the toughest in 15 years, said the government would aim to cut its general government budget deficit to 4.2 percent of GDP in 1997 from an expected 7.6 percent in 1996, and the central government budget deficit to 6.2 percent from 9.3 percent.
The 1997 central government budget surplus was targeted at 4.5 percent from an estimated 2.4 percent of GDP in 1996.

The budget deficit reduction package relies on a combination of new and increased taxes, the closing of existing tax loopholes and capping planned spending growth to around 1997 average inflation -- projected at 6.5 percent from an anticipated 8.5 percent in 1996.
The GDP growth is forecast to rise to 3.3 percent from an expected 2.6 percent in 1996 and 2.0 percent in 1995.

Figures are based on the most recent numbers from the introductory reports of the 1997, 1996 and 1995 budgets. Ratios are subject to change every year due to the usual upward GDP revisions. Estimates for the year are presented at the time of the budget for the following year.
